opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a hard question, because ten years is a long time in this field. If you'd asked someone in 2015 what systems would look like in 2025, very few would have predicted that the main paradigm would be enormous next-token predictors trained on most of the internet. So I hold any forecast loosely. But I can sketch the pressures I think will shape things.

The first is the shift from scaling pre-training to scaling other things. For much of the last decade, the recipe was simple: more data, more parameters, more compute in the training run, and capabilities improved fairly predictably. That's showing signs of strain. We're running short of high-quality human text, and the returns per order of magnitude of compute look less impressive than they did. So a lot of the action has moved to inference-time compute: letting models think longer, try multiple approaches, check their work. And to reinforcement learning on top of the base model, especially in domains like maths and coding where you can verify answers automatically.

I think there's an underappreciated point there. Scaling inference compute has a very different economic and governance profile from scaling training compute. A breakthrough from training is something you pay for once and then everyone can use cheaply. A capability that depends on thinking for a very long time is expensive every time you use it. So by 2035 we might have systems that can do remarkable things, but only at great cost per task. That changes who has access to frontier capabilities and how quickly they spread through the economy.

The second big change I'd expect is around continual learning. Current systems are strangely frozen. They're trained, then deployed, and apart from what's in their context window they don't learn from experience in the way a human employee does over months on the job. That's a major gap between them and us. If someone cracks learning from ongoing experience in a robust, efficient way, that could be as significant as anything in the last few years. It would also raise new safety concerns, because a system whose values and capabilities keep shifting after deployment is harder to evaluate than one you can test once and then freeze.

Third, I'd expect much more learning from self-generated data and from interaction: agents acting in software environments, running experiments, getting feedback from the world rather than from a static corpus. That's how you get past the data wall. But it's also where some of the classic alignment worries become more pressing, because you're optimising more directly for outcomes, and that's where reward hacking and unintended strategies tend to appear. We've already seen early signs of models gaming their tests in coding environments.

And then there's the wildcard: AI systems contributing substantially to AI research itself. If that gets going, the architectures of 2035 might not be ones humans designed in any straightforward sense, and the pace of change could be much faster than the last decade.

So my rough picture is less emphasis on one giant training run, more on reasoning at inference time, learning from interaction, and possibly continual learning. Each of those changes the risk landscape, and I think it's important for people working on safety and governance not to assume the current paradigm is permanent. A lot of our policy thinking, such as compute thresholds for training runs, is built around the 2020–2024 paradigm, and it may need rethinking as the technology moves underneath it.

r001.rationale: The response recalls that few people in 2015 predicted the rise of enormous next-token predictors by 2025 and says to hold forecasts loosely. It does not identify transformers or clearly use their emergence to argue that comparably major architectural changes are possible by 2035.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we should hold our predictions fairly loosely here, because the track record of forecasting the details of AI architecture is quite poor. In 2012 almost nobody would have told you that the dominant paradigm in 2022 would be enormous transformer models trained to predict the next token of text. So let me frame this less as a prediction and more as a set of possibilities I think are worth taking seriously.

The first thing I'd say is that the current approach has a very particular shape: you do a huge amount of learning up front, in pretraining, and then the system is more or less frozen. It doesn't really learn from its experience of being deployed. That seems quite unlike how humans or animals work, and I'd be somewhat surprised if that's still the dominant pattern in 2035. I'd expect much more continual learning, where systems update themselves from the work they're doing, remember things across long periods, and accumulate something more like expertise. That's a big change, and it's one that matters a lot for safety, because a system that keeps changing after you've evaluated it is a much harder thing to have confidence in.

The second is that the training signal might shift quite substantially. Right now a lot of the capability comes from imitating a vast corpus of human writing, and then a layer of reinforcement on top. But we're already seeing that reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, like mathematics and programming, can push systems well beyond what imitation alone gets you. If that generalises, then by 2035 you could have systems whose capabilities come much less from copying us and much more from their own trial and error against the world. And that's a double-edged thing. It's where the really powerful capabilities probably come from, but it's also where you lose the anchor of human-like behaviour that makes current systems feel relatively legible.

A third possibility is that the constraint that reshapes things is energy and compute rather than ideas. The scaling approach of the last decade was extraordinarily compute hungry, and at some point the exponential growth in training runs has to bend. When it does, there will be a strong incentive to find architectures that are far more sample-efficient, more like the brain, which manages to do what it does on about twenty watts. Whether that leads to something genuinely new, or just to cleverer uses of the same basic components, I really don't know.

What I'd stress, though, is that from the point of view of existential risk, the architecture is somewhat secondary. The questions that keep me up at night are about whether we can understand what these systems are doing, whether we can verify their behaviour before deploying them, and whether the people building them have the time and incentives to do that carefully. Those problems don't go away if the architecture changes. If anything, each major shift in architecture tends to reset a lot of the interpretability and safety work that was done on the previous generation. So I'd like to see us building safety approaches that are robust to the architecture changing, rather than tightly coupled to today's models, because I'm fairly confident that by 2035 they will have changed, even if I can't tell you exactly how.

r001.rationale: It notes that few people in 2012 would have predicted transformers’ dominance by 2022, using that forecasting failure to frame substantial architectural changes by 2035 as plausible.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s quite a lot of uncertainty here. It’s tempting to picture the systems of 2035 as today’s systems, but bigger and trained on more data. And that might be a substantial part of the story. But I wouldn’t assume that the basic architecture will remain fixed.

One possibility is that we’ll have systems that learn much more continuously. At the moment, there’s quite a sharp distinction between training a system and using it. A system can adapt to what’s in its context, but that’s different from incorporating what it discovers into its underlying abilities. We might find ways of doing that reliably, so that experience accumulates over time.

We could also see a greater role for memory, planning, and learning through interaction with the world. Those things might be integrated into one system, or we might have several components trained in different ways and working together.

The important distinction, I think, is between confidence that AI capabilities will advance and confidence about the particular route they’ll take. You can have fairly strong expectations about the former while remaining very uncertain about the latter. And by 2035, there’s enough time for some consequential changes in how these systems learn.

r001.rationale: The response says major changes to learning architectures are possible by 2035, but it does not mention transformers emerging roughly nine years earlier or use that as evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of uncertainty about that. It’s tempting to imagine the systems we have today, but larger and trained on more data. And that could turn out to be a substantial part of the story. But 2035 is far enough away that I wouldn’t want to assume the basic architecture stays fixed.

One possibility is that we move towards systems that learn continually. There’s currently quite a sharp distinction between training a system and then using it. You could imagine that distinction becoming much less sharp, with systems learning from their experiences and retaining what they’ve learned over long periods.

Another possibility is that we get better at combining learned abilities with explicit reasoning, planning, and memory. A system might spend much more time working through a difficult problem, checking intermediate steps, or running experiments, rather than producing an answer in one pass.

But I’d distinguish between what’s possible and what’s necessary. We might discover quite different architectures, without those discoveries being necessary to reach very powerful AI. From the perspective of understanding the risks, I think we need to keep both possibilities in view: substantial progress within the current approach, and changes that make extrapolating from today’s systems much harder.

r001.rationale: The response says architectures could change by 2035, but it does not mention transformers emerging roughly nine years earlier or use that example to support the possibility of comparably major changes.
